added_claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
added_claims.quote: getting closer to August and reversion of those rates moves you ended up reducing the rates exposure and then just before the the reversion INE equities uh you ended up kind of allocating a bit more to equities
added_claims.claim: Correlation-aware risk management cut equity risk in May-June while the short bond trade was reversing (two positively correlated longs), but as rates exposure was reduced approaching August the freed risk budget went back into equities just before the August reversal, so a risk-budget rule can add to the position that is about to reverse.
added_claims.indicator: correlation-based risk budgeting between equity and bond trend positions
added_claims.direction: equity exposure cut May-June then raised before the August 2024 reversal
added_claims.testable: yes - replay the risk-budget path through June-August 2024

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: they reduced they reduced risk mainly because of vol expansion not so much about the signal making a change for those few days
added_claims.claim: In the very fast August 2024 reversal, trend models cut exposure mainly through volatility scaling (volatility expansion), not through the trend signal changing within those few days.
added_claims.indicator: volatility-scaled position size versus trend signal
added_claims.direction: positions reduced by vol expansion, not signal flips
added_claims.conditions: very short sell-off with a V-shaped recovery
added_claims.testable: yes - decompose exposure change into vol-scaling and signal components

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: how you had handled the Yen the Nik over the summer months because there were signs of a change in direction or at least there were signs of those Trends being challenged
added_claims.claim: Results in the August 2024 reversal depended on how the yen and Nikkei positions had been handled over the summer, since those trends were already being challenged and were weaker than earlier in the year.
added_claims.indicator: yen and Nikkei trend strength, summer 2024
added_claims.testable: yes - attribute August 2024 P&L to yen and Nikkei positioning

added_claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
added_claims.quote: looking into August on a month that the market was positive doesn't even appear if you do your typical kind of Scar plot with a trend following smile
added_claims.claim: August 2024 was not a test of trend following's convexity (the 'smile' scatter of trend returns against equity returns): the downturn was too short-lived and the month ended positive, so convexity would only have paid if the move had been contagious and a fast model had reacted.
added_claims.indicator: trend-following smile (CTA returns vs equity returns)
added_claims.conditions: convexity needs a sustained, contagious downturn
added_claims.testable: yes - scatter of monthly CTA vs equity returns, label August 2024

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: there are more people who are now serious and who want to dive deeper into these type of strategies
added_claims.claim: August 2024 was a non-event for allocators, but events like 2022 opened discussions, so more asset owners are now serious about trend strategies and willing to act on their research.
added_claims.testable: partly - flows into CTA / trend products

added_claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
added_claims.quote: if you ask me I'm going to tell you zero because I have no clue and it shouldn't work in the first place
added_claims.claim: Asked what expected return to put into a mean-variance optimiser for trend following, Nick would say zero (no ex ante basis and it should not work in theory); yet using its historical Sharpe gives about 70% allocation, so optimiser inputs for trend are either unusable or absurd, which is why a different sizing method is needed.
added_claims.indicator: expected return input for trend following in mean-variance optimisation
added_claims.testable: partly - the optimiser output is a calculation; the zero input is a judgement

added_claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
added_claims.quote: people that don't feel comfortable about following is because it goes against their premises and their fundamental understanding of the market that you know past return should not predict future return
added_claims.claim: Citing Andrew's point: discomfort with trend following comes from the efficient-market premise that past returns should not predict future returns, but the empirical fact that they do cannot be ignored.

corrections.issue: Date error: the recording was on Friday 4 October 2024 (the EU EV-tariff vote is reported as 'this morning'), so the barometer reading of 36 'yesterday' was for Thursday 3 October; only the CTA index numbers are 'as of Wednesday night' (2 October).
corrections.fix: Niels' trend barometer finished at 36 on Thursday 3 October 2024 (weak); CTA indices as of Wednesday night 2 October: BTOP50 -78bp for October (+3.34% YTD), SG CTA -92bp (+1.56%), SG Trend about -1% for October (YTD garbled), short-term traders -63bp (-10bp YTD); MSCI World about -1.25% (+16% YTD), global sovereign bonds -8bp (+2.34%), S&P 500 about -1% (+19.5%).

corrections.issue: The condition 'gross of full costs' is unsupported: Niels says only that the 20-year fixed-lookback result is a simulation subject to the usual disclaimers; costs are discussed afterwards as a general trade-off by Nick, not as a statement about this simulation.
corrections.fix: Same claim, with condition 'simulated 20-year result, subject to simulation disclaimers; treatment of costs not stated'.

corrections.issue: Misstates the best CTA years. After Niels guessed 2022, 2014 and 2008, Nick says depending on the index variant 2002 is one of the top three and 2014 is the fourth ('those three plus one').
corrections.fix: Worst S&P years since 2000 were 2002, 2008 and 2022 (2022 also the worst bond year; GFC among the best bond years); the best CTA years were 2008, 2022 and (depending on index variant) 2002, with 2014 fourth.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker for part of the claim. Niels makes the debt-level point (40% in bonds may be too risky); the closing remark that 60/40 was a carry trade and a yield reduction at a turning point is Nick agreeing, and he asks which of those components can still exist.
corrections.fix: Niels: high government debt levels should be part of why 40% in bonds is too risky today. Nick (agreeing): 60/40 worked as a carry trade plus falling yields at a turning point, and it is an open question which of those components can persist.

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader captured the speed/V-shape analysis, three allocation papers and the sizing framework; missed several secondary points (risk-budget reallocation before August, vol-scaling versus signal change, convexity not tested, zero expected return input, EMH discomfort) and made one speaker split error and small date and ranking slips.
